talks.title: Welcome to fwd:cloudsec 2024!
talks.teaser: Aaron Zollman details Welcome to fwd:cloudsec 2024!.
talks.summary:
Overview: fwd:cloudsec organizers deliver the 2024 North America welcome address, declaring independence from co-location with re:Invent to preserve the conference's practitioner-focused community identity.

Key Topics: fwd:cloudsec's fifth year and first intentional scheduling separation from AWS re:Invent; the value of independent cloud security dialogue; commitment to open knowledge sharing; and building community for the next five years.

Technical Details: Organizers frame the scheduling change as deliberate independence, allowing open dialogue between researchers, developers, and practitioners without vendor conference dynamics influencing content or attendance.

Takeaways: Independent security conferences serve distinct community needs that vendor-adjacent events cannot fulfill. Practitioners should support communities prioritizing open dialogue over marketing.

talks.title: I'm Doing My Part! By Mapping Cloud Incidents to ATT&CK Techniques
talks.teaser: Casey Knerr examines I'm Doing My Part! By Mapping Cloud Incidents to ATT&CK Techniques.
talks.summary:
Why Map Cloud Incidents to ATT&CK

MITRE ATT&CK enterprise lead Casey Nur argues mapping threat reports to ATT&CK techniques enables a common language for sharing intelligence, spotting trends, and finding defensive gaps. ATT&CK Cloud spans IaaS, SaaS, Google Workspace, Office 365, and Azure AD (with ongoing cleanup as platforms evolve).

Three Mapping Questions

Analysts must extract atomic behaviors from prose, determine adversary goals to select tactics (often intertwined in cloud), then match techniques and sub-techniques using descriptions and keyword search. Multiple techniques may apply; perfection is less important than consistent community feedback.

Worked Example: Midnight Blizzard

Using Microsoft reporting on APT29/Midnight Blizzard, Nur isolates password spraying against a non-MFA test tenant with low-and-slow attempts to evade detection. She notes cloud mapping can feel repetitive when reports collapse to valid cloud accounts, but diverse techniques exist beyond that pattern when reports are parsed carefully.

talks.title: One Click, Six Services: Abusing The Dangerous Multi-service Orchestration Pattern
talks.teaser: Liv Matan investigates One Click, Six Services: Abusing The Dangerous Multi-service Orchestration Pattern.
talks.summary:
Hidden Cloud Dependencies

Tenable researcher Liv Matan explains how creating one GCP Cloud Function silently provisions storage buckets, Artifact Registry, Cloud Build, Cloud Run, and Eventarc triggers. This Jenga-like orchestration expands the attack surface beyond what operators see in the console.

Service Agents and Privilege Paths

Behind-the-scenes work runs under Google-managed service agents analogous to AWS service-linked roles or Azure managed identities. Second-generation Cloud Functions add complexity by combining Cloud Run and Eventarc, creating cross-service privilege-escalation opportunities such as Cloud Run access to container images.

Confused Function Vulnerability

Matan details a bounty-awarded flaw where permission to update a Cloud Function lets an attacker inject a malicious npm dependency into package.json. During deployment, Cloud Build installs it under the default Cloud Build service account, whose broad permissions can be stolen via IMDS credential exfiltration.

Defender Takeaways

GCP's mitigation lets customers choose custom service accounts for build and runtime, deprecates the legacy default Cloud Build account, and adds organization policies. Matan warns defaults remain dangerous and minimum permissions for deployment still leave residual risk across all major cloud providers.

talks.title: Forged in Fire: Forging Multi-Cloud Open Source Swiss-Army Knife
talks.teaser: Toni de la Fuente details Forged in Fire: Forging Multi-Cloud Open Source Swiss-Army Knife.
talks.summary:
Prowler's origin story

Tony deaa and Sergio Garcia from Prowler describe how a bash-based AWS audit script grew into a multi-cloud open-source security platform. They frame the core practitioner questions: what assets exist across clouds, where sensitive data lives, who has access, and how identity and resource relationships connect across accounts.

From bash to Python rewrite

The project gained traction after Black Hat EU Arsenal demos and thousands of GitHub stars. After the founder joined AWS, Prowler expanded AWS checks, then the team rewrote the tool in Python because shell portability across Linux, BSD, and macOS had become unmaintainable.

Multi-cloud Swiss army knife

Today Prowler targets consistent visibility and remediation workflows across providers, supporting automated fixes, click-ops, and scripted remediation. The talk positions open source as the right model for cloud security communities that need shared, auditable assessment tooling.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Toni de la Fuente, creator and CEO of Prowler, and Sergio Garcia, core maintainer, present the technical evolution and architectural lessons from building Prowler, a multi-cloud open-source security tool. Presented at fwd:cloudsec, the talk details how Prowler evolved from an AWS-focused Bash script into a multi-cloud Python engine supporting AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Kubernetes with nearly 600 security checks and over 8 million downloads.

Key Topics:
- Evolution of Prowler from a 2016 Bash script into an enterprise Python platform
- Standardization of disparate multi-cloud findings using OCSF and ASFF schemas
- SDK and API inconsistencies across AWS (Boto3), Azure SDKs, GCP, and Kubernetes
- Concurrency, rate-limit throttling mitigation, and agentless compliance mapping

Technical Details:
Prowler was initiated in 2016 as a single Bash script built atop the AWS CLI to automate the CIS AWS Benchmark 1.0. To overcome operating system portability issues (such as divergent core utilities between Linux, BSD, and macOS) and manage rapid feature expansion, the tool was entirely rewritten in Python. Expanding to multi-cloud required reconciling fundamentally inconsistent cloud resource hierarchies. The maintainers adopted the Open Cybersecurity Schema Format (OCSF) and AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF) to establish a unified data contract. In this model, AWS Account IDs, Azure Subscriptions, GCP Projects, and Kubernetes Clusters are mapped to a standardized `account_uid`, while Azure locations and Kubernetes namespaces are normalized into unified regional fields.

The speakers contrast the developer experience across cloud provider SDKs and APIs. AWS provides a mature, centralized SDK (`boto3`/`botocore`) featuring built-in paginators and configurable retry options (`max_retries`) that allow Prowler to handle API throttling during concurrent, multi-threaded regional scans. AWS also publishes a global JSON file detailing service-region availability, which Prowler queries via GitHub Actions to ensure scan coverage across commercial, GovCloud, and China partitions. Conversely, Azure requires dozens of fragmented client libraries with erratic versioning, causing frequent breaking dependencies managed via Dependabot, alongside asynchronous requirements for Microsoft Graph (`aioazure`). GCP requires asynchronous execution without native client paginators, requiring manual iteration and explicit error handling for disabled service APIs.

Compliance mapping presented another major engineering hurdle. Because regulatory frameworks (CIS, PCI DSS, MITRE ATT&CK) provide high-level requirements without cloud-specific implementation details, Prowler implemented a custom JSON compliance schema. This schema maps generic compliance requirements (such as storage encryption-at-rest) directly to technical checks across S3, RDS, Azure Blob, and GCP Cloud Storage. The architecture remains entirely agentless, utilizing least-privilege, read-only audit roles (e.g., SecurityAudit in AWS) to evaluate configurations, delivering findings through CSV, JSON, and interactive Plotly Dash dashboards.

Key Takeaways:
Developing multi-cloud security tooling requires strict abstraction layers and reliance on open data schemas like OCSF to prevent vendor lock-in and decouple assessment logic from provider APIs. Security teams should perform exhaustive multi-region and multi-partition scans by default, as unmonitored secondary regions frequently harbor rogue or forgotten cloud resources. When designing high-concurrency API scanners, developers must engineer adaptive retry mechanisms with exponential backoffs and continuous dependency integration to absorb frequent cloud SDK breaking changes.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)
